```{r}
#| label: setup

options(cli.num_colors = 1, cli.dynamic = FALSE, cli.progress_show_after = Inf)
```

[TMB](https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp) (Kristensen et al., 2016) compiles a
log-density written as a C++ template, and computes its gradient by automatic
differentiation. The gradient is exact, and nothing has to be derived by
hand. `inla_vanilla()` takes TMB's objective and gradient as they are, apart
from the sign: TMB minimises.

This article fits the industrialisation and political democracy model of
Bollen (1989), a structural equation model with 39 parameters. The article
[Speeding up with Rcpp](rcpp.html) describes the model, its unconstrained
parameterisation, the priors and their Jacobians, and writes the same
log-posterior in R and in C++. Here we write it as a TMB template.

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| message: false
library(inlavanilla)
data(PoliticalDemocracy, package = "lavaan")
```

## Data and parameters

The 11 indicators, in the order `x1`, `x2`, `x3`, `y1`, ..., `y8`, and the
six pairs with correlated residuals:

```{r}
#| label: data
ov <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", paste0("y", 1:8))
Y <- as.matrix(PoliticalDemocracy[, ov])

cov_pairs <- rbind(
  c("y1", "y5"),
  c("y2", "y4"),
  c("y2", "y6"),
  c("y3", "y7"),
  c("y4", "y8"),
  c("y6", "y8")
)
```

The 39 parameters, all on an unconstrained scale, in six blocks:

| Block | Number | Parameters | Prior |
|:------|-------:|:-----------|:------|
| `nu` | 11 | intercepts | $N(0, 32^2)$ |
| `lam` | 5 | loadings of `x2`, `x3`, and `a`, `b`, `c` | $N(0, 10^2)$ |
| `beta` | 3 | regressions | $N(0, 10^2)$ |
| `logv_lv` | 3 | log variance of `ind60`, log disturbance variances of `dem60` and `dem65` | $\text{Gamma}(1, \text{rate } 0.5)$ on the SD |
| `logv_ov` | 11 | log residual variances | $\text{Gamma}(1, \text{rate } 0.5)$ on the SD |
| `z` | 6 | residual correlations $\rho$ on the atanh scale | $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$ on $(\rho + 1)/2$ |

We give them readable names, and the same starting values as in the Rcpp
article:

```{r}
#| label: init
parnames <- c(
  paste0("nu_", ov),
  c("lam_x2", "lam_x3", "a", "b", "c"),
  c("beta_dem60_ind60", "beta_dem65_ind60", "beta_dem65_dem60"),
  paste0("logv_", c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")),
  paste0("logv_", ov),
  paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
init <- c(
  colMeans(Y),
  rep(1, 5),
  rep(0, 3),
  rep(0, 3),
  log(apply(Y, 2, var) / 2),
  rep(0, 6)
)
names(init) <- parnames
```

## The template

A TMB template declares its data and parameters, and returns the value to
minimise, here the negative log-posterior. `density::MVNORM_t` is TMB's
multivariate normal; it returns the negative log-density, normalising
constant included. The 75 pointwise log-likelihoods are kept in a vector, and
`REPORT()` makes them available from R. The log-prior adds the log-Jacobians
of the standard deviations and correlations, as in the Rcpp article.

```{r}
#| label: tmb-file
tmb_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "sem_tmb.cpp")
```

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = tmb_file, lang = "cpp")}
#include <TMB.hpp>

template <class Type>
Type objective_function<Type>::operator()() {
  DATA_MATRIX(Y);            // 75 x 11: x1, x2, x3, y1, ..., y8

  PARAMETER_VECTOR(nu);      // 11 intercepts
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(lam);     // loadings: x2, x3, then a, b, c
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(beta);    // dem60 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ dem60
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(logv_lv); // log variances of ind60, dem60, dem65
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(logv_ov); // log residual variances, x1 to y8
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(z);       // residual correlations, atanh scale

  int n = Y.rows(), p = Y.cols();

  // Loadings, with the first of each latent variable fixed at 1, and a, b, c
  // shared between 1960 and 1965
  matrix<Type> Lambda(p, 3);
  Lambda.setZero();
  Lambda(0, 0) = 1;
  Lambda(1, 0) = lam(0);
  Lambda(2, 0) = lam(1);
  Lambda(3, 1) = 1;
  Lambda(4, 1) = lam(2);
  Lambda(5, 1) = lam(3);
  Lambda(6, 1) = lam(4);
  Lambda(7, 2) = 1;
  Lambda(8, 2) = lam(2);
  Lambda(9, 2) = lam(3);
  Lambda(10, 2) = lam(4);

  matrix<Type> B(3, 3);
  B.setZero();
  B(1, 0) = beta(0);
  B(2, 0) = beta(1);
  B(2, 1) = beta(2);
  matrix<Type> I(3, 3);
  I.setIdentity();
  matrix<Type> A = atomic::matinv(matrix<Type>(I - B));

  vector<Type> psi = exp(logv_lv);
  vector<Type> v = exp(logv_ov);
  vector<Type> rho = tanh(z);
  matrix<Type> Psi = psi.matrix().asDiagonal();
  matrix<Type> Theta = v.matrix().asDiagonal();
  // Residual covariances: y1-y5, y2-y4, y2-y6, y3-y7, y4-y8, y6-y8
  int ci[6] = {3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8};
  int cj[6] = {7, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10};
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    Theta(ci[k], cj[k]) = rho(k) * sqrt(v(ci[k]) * v(cj[k]));
    Theta(cj[k], ci[k]) = Theta(ci[k], cj[k]);
  }

  matrix<Type> LA = Lambda * A;
  matrix<Type> Sigma = LA * Psi * LA.transpose() + Theta;

  // Pointwise log-likelihood
  density::MVNORM_t<Type> mvn(Sigma);
  vector<Type> loglik(n);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    vector<Type> r = vector<Type>(Y.row(i)) - nu;
    loglik(i) = -mvn(r);
  }
  REPORT(loglik);

  // Log-prior on the unconstrained scale, with the Jacobians
  Type logprior = sum(dnorm(nu, Type(0), Type(32), true)) +
    sum(dnorm(lam, Type(0), Type(10), true)) +
    sum(dnorm(beta, Type(0), Type(10), true));
  vector<Type> logv(14);
  logv << logv_lv, logv_ov;
  for (int k = 0; k < 14; k++) {
    // Gamma(1, rate 0.5) on the SD (TMB's dgamma() takes the scale), and
    // d SD / d logv = SD / 2
    Type sd = exp(logv(k) / Type(2));
    logprior += dgamma(sd, Type(1), Type(1 / 0.5), true) + log(sd / Type(2));
  }
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    // Beta(1, 1) on (rho + 1) / 2, and d rho / d z = 1 - rho^2
    Type u = (rho(k) + Type(1)) / Type(2);
    logprior += dbeta(u, Type(1), Type(1), true) - log(Type(2)) +
      log(Type(1) - rho(k) * rho(k));
  }

  return -(sum(loglik) + logprior);
}
```

## Compiling

`TMB::compile()` builds a shared library from the template, which takes a
minute or so. `TMB::MakeADFun()` then records the computation and returns an
object whose `fn` and `gr` evaluate the objective and its gradient. The
parameters go in as a list of the six vectors, and `obj$par` holds them in
one vector, in the same order as `init`.

```{r}
#| label: compile
#| message: false
invisible(TMB::compile(tmb_file))
dyn.load(TMB::dynlib(sub("\\.cpp$", "", tmb_file)))

blocks <- rep(
  c("nu", "lam", "beta", "logv_lv", "logv_ov", "z"),
  c(11, 5, 3, 3, 11, 6)
)
obj <- TMB::MakeADFun(
  data = list(Y = Y),
  parameters = split(unname(init), factor(blocks, unique(blocks))),
  DLL = "sem_tmb",
  silent = TRUE
)
all.equal(unname(obj$par), unname(init))
```

### A check against INLAvaan

INLAvaan fits the same model, with the same parameterisation and priors. As
in the Rcpp article, we put its posterior mode in our order:

```{r}
#| label: inlavaan
model <- "
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8
"
fit_inlavaan <- INLAvaan::asem(
  model,
  PoliticalDemocracy,
  meanstructure = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
int <- INLAvaan::get_inlavaan_internal(fit_inlavaan)

lv <- c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")
inlavaan_names <- c(
  paste0(ov, "~1"),
  "ind60=~x2",
  "ind60=~x3",
  "a",
  "b",
  "c",
  "dem60~ind60",
  "dem65~ind60",
  "dem65~dem60",
  paste0(c(lv, ov), "~~", c(lv, ov)),
  paste0(cov_pairs[, 1], "~~", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
at <- match(inlavaan_names, names(int$coefficients))
theta_inlavaan <- setNames(int$theta_star_novbc[at], parnames)
```

There, the template's objective should equal the one INLAvaan minimised:

```{r}
#| label: inlavaan-check
c(TMB = obj$fn(theta_inlavaan), INLAvaan = int$opt$objective)
```

## Fitting

TMB's `fn` returns the negative log-posterior and `gr` its gradient as a
one-row matrix, so we negate both and flatten the gradient. With `init` as
the starting values, the parameters keep our names; `obj$par` would also do,
and its repeated names (`nu`, `nu`, ...) would be numbered.

```{r}
#| label: fit
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  function(theta) -obj$fn(theta),
  init,
  grad = function(theta) -as.vector(obj$gr(theta))
)
```

`inla_vanilla()` checks the gradient against finite differences at `init`,
and would warn if it disagreed. The calls, and the time per call in
microseconds:

```{r}
#| label: speed
time_per_call <- function(f, n) {
  elapsed <- system.time(
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      f()
    }
  )[["elapsed"]]
  1e6 * elapsed / n
}
fit$counts
c(
  fn = time_per_call(function() obj$fn(init), n = 2000),
  gr = time_per_call(function() obj$gr(init), n = 1000)
)
```

A gradient costs a few evaluations of the objective, against 40 for finite
differences. Without it, the fit would take over 20,000 evaluations of the
objective. A hand-written gradient, as in the Rcpp article, can be faster
still, but it has to be derived and checked; TMB's needs neither.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: print
fit
```

This agrees with the Rcpp article's fit, which uses the same log-posterior,
to within about $10^{-4}$ posterior SDs. The two checks flagged by
`summary()` are the scan-path bend and the gap between the skew-normal and
VB means, both for `logv_dem65`; the [Rcpp article](rcpp.html) discusses
them.

```{r}
#| label: plot
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: "Posterior densities of the six residual correlations on the atanh scale, each close to a Gaussian, with the Laplace Gaussians dashed."
plot(fit, pars = paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2]))
```

### On the natural scale

The parameters are on the unconstrained scale, and `sampling()` with `fun`
maps its draws back. Here are the residual correlations $\rho = \tanh z$ and
the disturbance variance of `dem65`, next to the posterior medians from
INLAvaan's own copula draws, which are on the natural scale.

```{r}
#| label: natural
set.seed(2026)
natural <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 10000, fun = function(theta) {
  rho <- tanh(theta[paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])])
  names(rho) <- paste0("rho_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])
  c(rho, psi_dem65 = exp(theta[["logv_dem65"]]))
})
draws <- INLAvaan::sampling(fit_inlavaan, nsamp = 10000)
v <- function(x) draws[, paste0(x, "~~", x)]
rho <- draws[, paste0(cov_pairs[, 1], "~~", cov_pairs[, 2])] /
  sqrt(v(cov_pairs[, 1]) * v(cov_pairs[, 2]))
round(
  cbind(
    t(apply(natural, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))),
    INLAvaan = c(apply(rho, 2, median), median(v("dem65")))
  ),
  3
)
```

The medians agree with INLAvaan's, up to the Monte Carlo error of the two
sets of draws. The disturbance variance of `dem65` is small and poorly
determined, with a long right tail on this scale.

### Leave-one-out cross-validation

`obj$report()` evaluates the template at any parameter value without
recording derivatives, and returns the 75 pointwise log-likelihoods: the
`loglik` that `loo()` needs. It leaves out one country at a time, from this
one fit:

```{r}
#| label: loo
loo_sem <- loo(fit, function(theta) obj$report(theta)$loglik)
loo_sem
```

INLAvaan's `loo()` uses the same deterministic expansion (Alhyari et al.,
2026), with its own per-case log-likelihoods:

```{r}
#| label: loo-inlavaan
loo_inlavaan <- INLAvaan::loo(fit_inlavaan)
round(
  rbind(
    ours = loo_sem$estimates[, "Estimate"],
    INLAvaan = loo_inlavaan$estimates[, "Estimate"]
  ),
  2
)
```

The two agree to well within the standard error. They differ a little because
each expands about its own VB-corrected mean, and the two VB corrections take
their expectations with different rules.

With 39 parameters this takes $39^2 + 39 + 1$, or 1,561, evaluations of the
template, each giving all 75 terms. See
[Model comparison with LOO and WAIC](model-comparison.html) for what the
numbers mean and how to compare models with them.
